title: Black Canyon of the Gunnison
subtitle: COLORADO'S DEEPEST SECRET

scenes.text: In some places, this canyon is only forty feet wide at the river, and more than seventeen hundred feet deep. Most people have never heard of it.
This is Black Canyon of the Gunnison, in western Colorado. People say it earned its name from the deep shadows that fill the narrow gorge.
The whole canyon runs forty eight miles. Fourteen of those miles are inside the national park, and that is where the walls get truly extreme.
This is the Painted Wall. From the river to the rim it stands two thousand, two hundred and fifty feet. It is the highest cliff in Colorado, and it is taller than the Empire State Building.
Look closely, and you can see pale veins running through the dark rock, like someone drew on the wall.
The rock at the bottom is nearly two billion years old. About sixty million years ago, an uplift pushed it up toward the sky. Then, about thirty million years ago, volcanoes buried it again.
Then, as early as two million years ago, the Gunnison River began flowing in force. It sliced down through the volcanic rock, and kept cutting into the ancient stone beneath.
And it is still carving. By the park's own estimate, the canyon erodes about one inch every hundred years.

This river is not lazy. Across the park, the Gunnison drops around two thousand one hundred feet in just fourteen miles. At the steepest stretch, near Chasm View, it falls two hundred and forty feet in a single mile.
At the Narrows, the canyon squeezes to just forty feet across at the river, with walls rising more than seventeen hundred feet on either side.
From the rim, a string of overlooks opens onto the drop. Most of them look straight down into a gorge that seems to have no bottom.
Away from the edge, sagebrush trails wind along the rim, with the canyon always just beside you.
In winter, snow dusts the rim, and the whole place goes quiet, as if the canyon is holding its breath, waiting for spring.
When the sun goes down, the park turns into something else. In twenty fifteen it was designated an International Dark Sky Park, a place where the night stays naturally dark.
Wait for the right light, and the Painted Wall glows orange at dawn, while the depths below stay in deep shadow.
This land was first protected as a national monument in nineteen thirty three, and it later became a national park.

Right here in the canyon, workers once dug the Gunnison Tunnel, five point eight miles through solid rock, to carry river water to farms in the valley. It was dedicated on September twenty third, nineteen oh nine.
Unlike the giants of the park system, this place rarely makes anyone's top ten list. That is part of what makes it feel like a secret.
So here is my question. Would you stand right at the edge of a drop this deep, or would you keep a few steps back? Tell me in the comments.
